issues.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument is not legally proved when the attesting witness examined fails to establish that the required witnesses attested it in the legally prescribed manner.
material_facts: The proceeding concerned applications for probate of competing wills, and the disputed will was required to be attested by two witnesses.

Only one of the two named attesting witnesses was examined. He testified that the testator signed in his presence, but did not establish that the other named witness had attested the will in the required manner; his account was inconsistent with the will’s recital that the testator signed before both witnesses and both then signed.
The will named the other attesting witness as executor, but it was produced from the custody of the witness who testified, and that custody was not explained.
The will’s author and typist were unknown. The propounders had previously asserted in other proceedings that the testator had left no will, and did not explain that assertion in the probate evidence.

The will left the entire property to the propounders, who were not Class I heirs, excluding the testator’s sister; the sister had lived near and cared for the testator, while the propounders lived elsewhere.
The Court found numerous suspicious circumstances on the face of the will and in the evidence, in addition to the failure to prove the statutory requirements for execution.
issues.conclusion: The will dated 18 June 1995 was not legally proved. The judgment granting probate of it could not stand, and the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, an unprivileged will must be attested by two or more witnesses, each satisfying the prescribed witnessing and signing requirements. Section 68 of the Evidence Act permits proof by examining at least one attesting witness, but that witness must establish due execution, including the required attestation by both witnesses; if the witness examined does not do so, an available other attesting witness must be called to complete the proof. A testator’s signature alone does not prove due execution. The propounder must also satisfy the court that the will is ordinarily free from genuine suspicious circumstances and remove such circumstances. The Court applied Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam, Benga Behera v. Braja Kishore Nanda, Ramabai Padmakar Patil v. Rukminibai Vishnu Vekhande, Anil Kak v. Kumari Sharada Raje, and Babu Singh v. Ram Sahai; it also referred to Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act for the meaning of attestation.

predicates.probate_proceeding: A person sought probate of a testamentary instrument.
predicates.testamentary_instrument_requires_two_att: The testamentary instrument was subject to a requirement that two witnesses attest it in the prescribed manner.
predicates.only_one_attesting_witness_examined: The person seeking probate examined only one of the instrument’s attesting witnesses.
predicates.examined_witness_failed_to_prove_attesta: The attesting witness examined did not establish that both required witnesses attested the instrument in the prescribed manner.
predicates.will_not_legally_proved: The court ruled that the testamentary instrument had not been legally proved.

issues.definition: When probate is sought for an instrument requiring attestation by two witnesses, but the sole attesting witness examined fails to prove that both witnesses attested it as required, the instrument is not legally proved.
